entry.englishMeaning: a formal event marking the opening of a building or project by cutting a ribbon
entry.coreIdea: Cut a ribbon to mark an official opening.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Literal event name: an opening ceremony in which cutting a ribbon marks the start of a building's or project's public use.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Usually celebratory because it marks an opening or achievement; the phrase does not say how important the project is.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Matter-of-fact here: the sentence simply states that someone will attend.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Standard wording in event announcements and local news; a general audience usually understands it without explanation.

when_to_use: Describe an opening event where a ribbon is ceremonially cut, such as the opening of a library or health centre.
when_not_to_use: Do not call every opening party a ribbon-cutting ceremony; use opening ceremony if you do not know whether a ribbon will be cut.

advanced_nuance: A ribbon-cutting ceremony symbolically marks an opening; an inauguration can include broader formal proceedings and speeches.
A ribbon-cutting ceremony marks an opening symbolically; its date does not necessarily prove when construction finished or ordinary service first began.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Picture scissors cutting a ribbon across the entrance to a new library.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: A ribbon-cutting ceremony marked the opening of the health centre.
memory_practice.recall_question: What action gives a ribbon-cutting ceremony its name?
memory_practice.recognition_task: Which event fits? A: Guests cut a ribbon to mark a new library opening. B: Staff meet to discuss next year’s budget. Explain your choice.
memory_practice.production_task: Write a short invitation to the opening of a fictional community centre. Mention the ribbon-cutting ceremony and its starting time.

examples.example_1: The mayor attended the ribbon-cutting ceremony for the new library.
examples.example_2: A ribbon-cutting ceremony marked the opening of the health centre.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: When does the new library open?
B: There is a ribbon-cutting ceremony at ten, followed by a public tour.
A: I will arrive a little early.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: He'll  be here  for  the  ribbon- cutting  cerem ony.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: a formal event marking the opening of a building or project by cutting a ribbon
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The speaker says he will attend the event marking an opening. The short quotation does not identify the building or project.

mistakes_differences.correction: Say: The mayor attended the ribbon-cutting ceremony, or a ribbon-cutting ceremony if it has not been identified.
mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Incorrect: The mayor attended ribbon-cutting ceremony. A singular ceremony needs a determiner.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: A ribbon-cutting ceremony symbolically marks an opening; an inauguration can include broader formal proceedings and speeches.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: hold / attend + a ribbon-cutting ceremony + for + opening

semanticReview.finding: Useful opening examples, collocations and inauguration contrast retained; generic dialogue, practice and filler nuance corrected. Exact OCR quotation preserved.

entry.tamilMeaning: தன்னைப் பற்றிய அளவுக்கு மீறிய திருப்தியுடனும் தற்பெருமையுடனும்
entry.coreIdea: A satisfied smile that suggests I am better than you.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Abstract adverb for behaving with excessive self-satisfaction or a sense of superiority.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Negative: it suggests that the person's satisfaction is irritating or undeserved.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Accusatory here: “always,” “skulking” and the claim that she thinks you are a slob create a strongly critical portrayal.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Common in descriptive writing and personal criticism. It makes a judgement about attitude, so use observable behaviour in diplomatic feedback.

when_to_use: Describe a smile, remark or manner that seems excessively pleased with itself, often at another person’s expense.
when_not_to_use: Do not use smugly for all happiness or pride; it adds criticism of the person’s attitude.
For neutral reporting, describe the words or behaviour instead of assuming that you know the person’s private thoughts.

advanced_nuance: Smugly expresses the narrator’s interpretation of a manner; it does not let the narrator know another person’s thoughts with certainty.
Someone can behave smugly while being right about the facts. The criticism concerns the self-satisfied attitude, not necessarily the answer.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Picture an irritating I told you so smile.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: He grinned smugly after predicting the result correctly.
memory_practice.recall_question: Why does smugly sound more critical than happily?
memory_practice.recognition_task: Which best fits smugly? A: Quietly thanking a team for their help. B: Smiling while saying I was right and the rest of you were clueless. Explain the attitude.
memory_practice.production_task: Write a two-line exchange in which a fictional character speaks smugly after a correct prediction. Make the self-satisfaction clear.

examples.example_1: He smiled smugly when the answer proved him right and everyone else wrong.
examples.example_2: I knew you would need my help, she said smugly as she opened the instruction manual.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: Why did his answer annoy you?
B: He said smugly that he was the only one who understood the problem.
A: He could have explained it without putting everyone else down.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: She's  always  smugly  skulking  around  the  house,  thinking  you're  a  slob.
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The speaker portrays her as excessively pleased with herself and looking down on someone else. This is the speaker’s judgement, not independent proof of what she thinks.

mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Incorrect: He smiled smug. An adverb is needed to describe how he smiled.
mistakes_differences.correction: Say He smiled smugly. Use the adjective in He looked smug.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Proudly can show understandable pleasure in an achievement. Smugly usually criticizes excessive self-satisfaction or superiority.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: smile/grin smugly; say something smugly; smugly + adjective

semanticReview.finding: Negative evaluative force distinguished from happiness and factual correctness; source mind-reading treated as speaker judgement.
semanticReview.scope: All eight sections and changed headers; no audio or local import verification.

entry.englishMeaning: with only a small amount of money available to spend
entry.coreIdea: Picture a small purse that must cover a whole list of costs.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Figurative expression for having little money available: “tight” presents the spending limit as restrictive.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Neutral about the people involved; it indicates financial constraint rather than automatically implying poverty or poor planning.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Practical here: the sentence gives a limitation affecting how the celebration is organized.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Common conversational and workplace English. “With limited funds” is a more formal alternative.

when_to_use: Suggest an affordable alternative to an expensive outing.
A natural model: I am on a tight budget this month, so could we have lunch at home?
when_not_to_use: Do not use on a tight budget to describe a short time limit; use a tight deadline for that.
Do not assume this means someone is poor: the available money may be limited for just this event or period.

advanced_nuance: on a tight budget: It is a natural way to set a spending boundary without revealing exact income.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Picture a small purse that must cover a whole list of costs.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: I am on a tight budget this month, so could we have lunch at home?
memory_practice.production_task: Suggest an affordable alternative to an expensive outing. Use the target expression in one or two sentences. Check its pattern and register only after speaking.
memory_practice.recall_question: Without looking, retrieve the expression meaning with only a small amount of money available to spend. Then say it in a new situation.
memory_practice.recognition_task: Choose the natural sentence. A: We are on a tight budget. B: We are in a tight budget. Explain why, then check the correction after answering.

examples.scenario: We are organising the celebration on a tight budget.
examples.another_setting: I am on a tight budget this month, so could we have lunch at home?

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: I am on a tight budget this month, so could we have lunch at home?
B: Of course; I can bring something to share.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: We are organising the celebration on a tight budget.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: with only a small amount of money available to spend
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The organisers have only limited money for the celebration, so their choices must keep costs low.

mistakes_differences.correction: We are on a tight budget.
mistakes_differences.common_mistake: We are in a tight budget.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: A tight budget limits spending; a tight deadline limits time.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: on a tight budget: be/live/travel + on a tight budget
common_collocations: plan a wedding on a tight budget

semanticReview.finding: Natural cost-boundary examples, coherent dialogue, on/in correction and practice retained; when-not-to-use field now gives actual restrictions.

entry.tamilMeaning: கிளை விதிகளின் மூலம் முடிவு செய்யும் கணிப்பு மாதிரி
entry.englishMeaning: a predictive model that makes decisions through branching rules
entry.coreIdea: Follow a sequence of branching questions to reach a prediction.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Technical model name: a predictive system follows branching rules, resembling the branching structure of a tree.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Neutral: the name describes a model structure, not its accuracy or fairness.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Instructional here: the speaker uses maximum depth to explain a decision tree's adjustable settings.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Standard machine-learning terminology. A general audience benefits from “a model that follows a sequence of branching questions.”

when_to_use: Name a predictive model that follows branching rules learned from examples.
Use it when discussing how a model splits data or how limiting its depth changes its complexity.
when_not_to_use: Do not use decision tree as a general name for all machine-learning models.
Keep this lesson’s predictive-model sense separate from a hand-drawn planning diagram used to weigh personal choices.

advanced_nuance: A decision tree can predict a category or a numerical value. The word decision does not restrict it to yes/no output.
A deeper decision tree can fit more detail, including noise. Greater depth does not automatically improve predictions on new data.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Picture a branching path ending in a predicted answer.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: The decision tree asks successive questions before predicting a category.
memory_practice.recall_question: What does maximum depth limit in a decision tree?
memory_practice.recognition_task: Which describes a decision tree? A: A predictive model that follows branching rules. B: A list of unrelated project deadlines. Explain your choice.
memory_practice.production_task: Explain to a colleague how a decision tree could classify support messages. Use train a decision tree and name the categories it would predict.

examples.example_1: We trained a decision tree to classify incoming support messages by topic.
examples.example_2: The researcher used a decision tree to predict a building’s energy consumption from its size and insulation.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: Why did you limit the decision tree’s depth?
B: The deeper version fitted the training data closely but performed worse on new examples.
A: Let’s compare both versions on the validation set.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: For example, if you are using a decision tree, one important hyperparameter is the maximum depth of the tree, meaning how many levels is the tree allowed to split.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: a predictive model that makes decisions through branching rules
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The source describes limiting how many levels a decision tree may have. Its branches apply rules that lead to a prediction.

mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Incorrect: We trained decision tree to classify the messages. The singular countable noun phrase needs a determiner.
mistakes_differences.correction: Say We trained a decision tree to classify the messages.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: A decision tree is one predictive model with branching rules. A random forest combines many trees; the names are not interchangeable.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: train a decision tree on + data; use a decision tree to + predict/classify
common_collocations: limit the depth of a decision tree

semanticReview.finding: Branching predictive-model sense, countable noun grammar and coherent validation dialogue checked; classification/regression and overfitting checked against scikit-learn documentation.
semanticReview.scope: All eight sections and changed headers; no audio or local import verification.

entry.tamilMeaning: ஒரு யோசனையை கருத்து அல்லது ஒப்புதலுக்காக ஒருவரிடம் முன்வைத்தல்
entry.englishMeaning: to present an idea to someone for their opinion or approval
entry.coreIdea: Slide the idea past another pair of eyes.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Abstract phrasal verb for asking someone to consider an idea; here, obtain feedback before sending a proposal.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Collaborative: it invites another person's judgement without necessarily making a formal approval request.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Polite and consultative here: “Can I” asks permission to seek the listener's opinion.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Conversational, especially in workplace exchanges. “Ask for your feedback on” is clearer in formal correspondence.

when_to_use: Ask for another person’s reaction or informal review before acting on an idea. Say whether you need comments or a definite approval.
when_not_to_use: Run an idea by someone asks for a reaction or approval; inform someone simply gives them information.

advanced_nuance: run by: It is conversational; seek review or request approval makes the required authority clearer in formal communication.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Slide the idea past another pair of eyes.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: I ran the holiday dates by my family before making the booking.
memory_practice.production_task: Use “run by” in your own response: Ask a specialist to check a proposal before you send it, stating the feedback needed.
memory_practice.recall_question: Without looking at the heading, recall the expression meaning “to present an idea to someone for their opinion or approval”. Then explain it in your own words.
memory_practice.recognition_task: Compare these two statements and choose the accurate form or interpretation. A: “I want to run by you an idea.” B: “I want to run an idea by you.” Explain the difference before checking Mistakes & Differences.

examples.workplace: Can I run this proposal by you before I send it?
examples.another_context: I ran the holiday dates by my family before making the booking.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: Can I run this proposal by you before I send it?
B: Of course. Do you want me to check the figures or the wording?
A: The figures, please, especially the delivery costs.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: Can I run this proposal by you before I send it?
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: to present an idea to someone for their opinion or approval
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The speaker wants the listener to consider the proposal and give feedback before it is sent.

mistakes_differences.correction: I want to run an idea by you.
mistakes_differences.common_mistake: I want to run by you an idea.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Run an idea by someone asks for a reaction or approval; inform someone simply gives them information.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: run by: run + idea + by + person; run it by + person

semanticReview.finding: Replaced mismatched reply with a direct response and clarification; valid separable pattern, examples, Tamil and review-versus-information contrast retained.
